answer: I'd like to talk about the first really expensive thing I ever bought for myself. A time I spent money on something genuinely special was when I bought my first proper laptop with money I had saved myself. It was during my second year at university, and I paid for it with the money I earned from private tuition, teaching two schoolchildren in the evenings. It took me months of careful budgeting, as it was a significant amount for me at the time. I had to be quite [[frugal]], cutting back on unnecessary spending to reach my goal. I kept a small notebook where I wrote down every taka I saved. I stopped eating out, walked instead of taking rickshaws, and said no to a few trips with friends. When I finally had enough and walked into the shop to buy it, the feeling was incredibly [[satisfying]]. It was a mid-range model, nothing fancy, but to me it felt like the most valuable thing in the world. What made it so special was that I had earned it entirely through my own effort and patience, without asking my father for anything. It was not just a purchase; it felt like a genuine [[accomplishment]]. The laptop went on to become essential for my studies and work, so it turned out to be a wise investment too. Honestly, buying something you have saved hard for feels far more rewarding than a casual, [[impulsive]] purchase. That experience taught me the value of patience and [[delayed gratification]], a lesson I still carry with me.

followUps.q: Do you still have that laptop?
followUps.answer: I do, although it is quite slow now. My younger sister used it for her studies for a while, and these days it mostly sits on my desk at home for watching cricket highlights.

followUps.q: Are you good at saving money now?
followUps.answer: Reasonably good, yes. I put a little aside every month, partly because I would like to study abroad one day, and that goal makes it much easier to resist unnecessary spending.

note: Added private tuition as the source of savings and concrete cutbacks; 'rewarding' unmarked, marked 'impulsive' and 'delayed gratification'.
